entries.title: AML/CFT
entries.body: The fight against money laundering and the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) refers to the regulatory measures adopted to prevent the use of Bitcoin in illegal activities. These measures include identifying and verifying the identity of customers (KYC), monitoring transactions to detect “suspicious” patterns, and cooperating with the authorities to report activities considered illegal. Regulated exchange platforms are required to comply with them in order to operate in many jurisdictions, notably in France.

entries.title: DISCRETE LOGARITHM
entries.body:
The discrete logarithm is a mathematical problem that is used in certain public-key cryptographic algorithms. In a cyclic group of order `q`, with a generator `g`, if we have an equation of the form `g^x = h`, then `x` is called the discrete logarithm of `h` with respect to the base `g`, modulo `q`. In simple terms, it involves determining the exponent `x` when `g`, `h`, and `q` are known. The discrete logarithm is therefore the inverse of exponentiation in a finite cyclic group. However, for large values of `q`, solving the discrete logarithm problem is considered algorithmically hard. This property is exploited to ensure the security of many cryptographic protocols, such as the Diffie-Hellman protocol for key exchange. 

The discrete logarithm is also used in elliptic curve cryptography (ECC), among others in the ECDSA algorithm (*Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm*). In the context of elliptic curves, the discrete logarithm problem extends to finding a scalar `k` such that `k \cdot G = K`, where `G` and `K` are points on the curve, and `\cdot` represents the point multiplication operation. In the context of Bitcoin, scripts can use either ECDSA or the Schnorr protocol in order to lock UTXOs. They both rely on the infeasibility of computing the discrete logarithm.

entries.title: GRESHAM'S LAW
entries.body:
Economic principle according to which “bad money drives out good”. When two currencies circulate simultaneously with an imposed legal tender status, economic agents tend to hoard the one that retains its value and to spend first the one that is depreciating. The lower-quality currency then dominates exchanges, while the superior currency disappears from circulation.

This phenomenon was formulated by the English financier Thomas Gresham in 1558, in a letter to Queen Elizabeth I, to describe the state of degradation of English silver coins resulting from the Great Debasement carried out under Henry VIII and Edward VI (1544–1551). It has historically been observed whenever a state imposes an artificial parity between two forms of money: coins with a high precious metal content are melted down, exported or hoarded, while the debased coins continue to circulate.

In the context of Bitcoin, some invoke Gresham's law to explain why bitcoiners prefer to spend fiat currencies, perceived as depreciating, rather than their bitcoins, perceived as appreciating. According to this reading, bitcoin plays the role of the hoarded “good money”, and fiat currencies are spent first, which reinforces bitcoin's role as a store of value at the expense of its use as a means of payment.

However, this application is disputed. Strictly speaking, Gresham's law assumes an imposed legal tender status or a fixed exchange rate between the two currencies, a condition absent between bitcoin and fiat currencies, which trade freely on the markets. Moreover, other, more prosaic factors explain why bitcoin is little spent: in many jurisdictions, every spending of bitcoin constitutes a taxable event subject to capital gains tax, which discourages its everyday use; furthermore, the number of merchants accepting bitcoin remains very limited, making its use as payment simply impractical.

entries.title: ISSUANCE LIMIT
entries.body: The ceiling set for the total money supply of BTC, established at approximately 21 million units. This limit is defined by the inflation policy in the Bitcoin protocol. New BTC are created and distributed to miners via the subsidy for validating each block. This subsidy is cut in half every 210,000 blocks, a process known as the “*halving*”. This method guarantees that monetary creation will gradually decrease until it reaches zero.

entries.title: L402
entries.body:
L402, formerly known as LSAT (*Lightning Service Authentication Token*), is an authentication and payment standard for distributed services. It takes its name from the HTTP status code 402 (*Payment Required*). L402 combines two mechanisms: macaroons, which are bearer authentication tokens that can be verified with simple cryptography and no centralized database, and the Lightning Network, which provides an instant payment system.

L402 works by associating a macaroon with the hash of a Lightning payment. When a user wants to access a protected service, the service hands them a macaroon along with a Lightning invoice. Once the payment is made, the user obtains the preimage which, combined with the macaroon, forms a valid L402 credential. The service does not need to directly check whether the invoice has been paid: simply presenting a preimage that matches the payment hash is enough to prove settlement.

L402 is implemented in Aperture, a reverse proxy developed by Lightning Labs, which handles the issuance of macaroons and invoices, then forwards authenticated requests to the protected APIs.

entries.title: LABEL
entries.body: A tag or annotation assigned to a UTXO in a Bitcoin wallet to remember where it came from. For example, if I own a UTXO coming from a P2P purchase on Bisq with Charles, I could give it the label “`Non-KYC Bisq Charles`”. This is a good practice that helps remember the origin or intended destination of that UTXO, which makes managing funds and optimizing privacy easier. *Labelling* is all the more important when it is used with *coin control*. Indeed, by allowing users to differentiate and precisely select UTXOs for their transactions, this practice helps avoid merging UTXOs coming from different sources. This limits the risks associated with the CIOH (*Common Input Ownership Heuristic*) chain analysis heuristic, which can reveal the common ownership of a transaction's inputs.

entries.title: LABEL - SILENT PAYMENTS
entries.body:
In the Silent Payments protocol, labels are integers used to modify the initial static address in order to create many other static addresses. Using these labels makes it possible to segregate payments sent via Silent Payments, by using a different static address for each purpose, without excessively increasing the operational burden of detecting these payments (scanning). Bob uses a static address `B`, made up of two public keys: `B_{scan}` for scanning and `B_{spend}` for spending. The hash of `b_{scan}` and an integer `m`, scalar-multiplied by the generator point `G`, is added to the spend public key `B_{spend}` to create a sort of new spend public key `B_m`:
```math
B_m\ =\ B_{spend}\ +\ hash(b_{scan}\ \Vert\ m) \cdot G
```
For example, the first key `B_1` is obtained this way:
```math
B_1\ =\ B_{spend}\ +\ hash(b_{scan}\ \Vert\ 1) \cdot G
```
The static address published by Bob will from now on be made up of `B_{scan}` and `B_m`. For example, the first static address with the label `1` will be:
```math
B\ =\ B_{scan}\ \Vert\ B_1
```
We only start from the label `1`, because the label `0` is reserved for change. Alice, who wants to send bitcoins to the labeled static address provided by Bob, will derive the unique payment address `P_0` using the new `B_1` in place of `B_{spend}`:
```math
P_0\ =\ B_1\ +\ hash(inputHash \cdot a \cdot B_{scan}\ \Vert\ 0) \cdot G
```
In reality, Alice does not even necessarily know that Bob has a labeled address, because she simply uses the second part of the static address he gave her, and in this case, it is the value `B_1` rather than `B_{spend}`. To scan for payments, Bob will always use the value of his initial static address with `B_{spend}` in this way:
```math
P_0\ =\ B_{spend}\ +\ hash(inputHash \cdot b_{scan} \cdot A\ \Vert\ 0) \cdot G
```
Then, he will simply subtract the value he finds for `P_0` from each output one by one. He then checks whether one of the results of these subtractions matches the value of one of the labels he uses in his wallet. If it matches, for example, for output #4 with the label `1`, it means that this output is a Silent Payment associated with his labeled static address `B_1`:
```math
Out_4\ -\ P_0\ =\ hash(b_{scan}\ \Vert\ 1) \cdot G
```
This works because:
```math
B_1\ =\ B_{spend}\ +\ hash(b_{scan}\ \Vert\ 1) \cdot G
```
Thanks to this method, Bob can use a multitude of static addresses (with `B_1`, `B_2`, `B_3`...), all derived from his base static address (`B\ =\ B_{scan}\ \Vert\ B_{spend}`), in order to keep different uses clearly separate. 

Be careful, however: this separation of static addresses only applies from the standpoint of personal wallet management, and does not separate identities. Since they all share the same `B_{scan}`, it is very easy to associate all the static addresses together and deduce that they belong to a single entity.

entries.title: LATENCY
entries.body: The delay between the sending and the receipt of a piece of information. In computing, it represents the time needed for data to travel between two computers. In the context of Bitcoin, latency can be studied in terms of the delay in propagating blocks across the network. High latency can put isolated miners at a disadvantage, because they keep working on blocks already invalidated by new blocks until they have received those new blocks. Latency therefore naturally pushes miners to pool together. It also reduces the overall security of the system by wasting the search for a valid proof of work. The purpose of setting a 10-minute period between each block is a measure to reduce the impact of latency on the system.

entries.title: LBTC - LIQUID BITCOIN
entries.body: Ticker symbol (*ticker*) that designates the bitcoin circulating on the Liquid Network, the federated sidechain developed by Blockstream. Each L-BTC is created through a two-way peg process (*peg-in*): BTC are locked on the main chain in an address controlled by the federation, and an equivalent amount of L-BTC is issued on Liquid. The reverse operation (*peg-out*) destroys the L-BTC on Liquid and releases the corresponding BTC on the main chain.

entries.title: LDK - LIGHTNING DEV KIT
entries.body: A software development kit (SDK) for Lightning. LDK is a collection of libraries and tools intended for developers to easily integrate Lightning into their software or to build Lightning applications while reducing complexity. LDK handles the complex aspects of integrating Lightning-related features. This project was launched by Spiral, a company created by Jack Dorsey, and was built on Rust-Lightning (RL).

entries.title: LEDGER
entries.body: A name sometimes used to designate the public, distributed register that records all the transactions made on Bitcoin, that is, the blockchain. Publishing and recording transactions on the *ledger* prevents double spending on Bitcoin, by ensuring that each coin a transaction tries to spend has not already been used before in another transaction.

entries.title: LEDGER - COMPANY
entries.body: A French company founded in 2014 that manufactures *hardware wallets* to secure bitcoin private keys. Its devices embed a certified security chip (*Secure Element*) that isolates the keys from any environment connected to the Internet.

entries.title: LEVELDB
entries.body: A lightweight, fast, open-source key-value storage library designed by Google. It is used in Bitcoin to store the UTXO set and the block index. This database system was introduced in 2012 as part of the “*Ultraprune*” Pull Request aimed at replacing BerkeleyDB. This change had significant repercussions, notably an unintentional hard fork with a major reorganization of 24 blocks on March 12, 2013. This incident was detailed in BIP-0050. Subsequently, the temporary rule limiting *locks* introduced in version 0.8.1 expired on May 15, 2013, resulting in a planned hard fork.

entries.title: LIANA
entries.body: *Open source* Bitcoin wallet management software developed by the company Wizardsardine (founded by Kevin Loaec and Antoine Poinsot). Liana stands out for its use of Miniscript to enable advanced, highly customizable security setups, notably recovery mechanisms based on *timelocks*. For example, a user can define a primary key for everyday spending, then one or more recovery keys that only become active after a defined period of inactivity. This model makes it possible to set up inheritance plans or automatic backup mechanisms without a trusted third party. Liana is compatible with *hardware wallets* that support Miniscript.

entries.title: LIBBITCOIN
entries.body:
A set of libraries written in C++ designed to build Bitcoin-related applications. Libbitcoin offers independent foundations for developing mobile applications, software and other systems around Bitcoin. Libbitcoin therefore has a modular architecture. All of the project's libraries are distributed under the free AGPL license.

Launched in 2011 by a team of developers led by Amir Taaki, Libbitcoin was then the second complete implementation of Bitcoin, after Satoshi's original client. Today, Eric Voskuil is the main maintainer and the most active contributor to the project.

entries.title: LIBERTY RESERVE
entries.body:
A digital currency service based in Costa Rica, founded by Arthur Budovsky in 2006. It allowed users to create accounts with minimal identity verification and to transfer funds denominated in “Liberty Reserve Dollars” (LR) or in euros. The service became popular for illicit transactions because of the anonymity it offered. At its peak, Liberty Reserve had more than one million users worldwide and is said to have processed about 55 million transactions.

In May 2013, the US government seized the service and indicted its operators, accused of having laundered more than 6 billion dollars. Together with the earlier shutdown of e-gold, this episode confirmed that centralized digital currency systems remain vulnerable to state intervention. Bitcoin, thanks to its decentralized architecture that spreads risk among its participants, aims to resist this type of shutdown.

entries.title: LIBSECP256K1
LIBWALLY-CORE
entries.body:
An *open source* cryptographic and utility library developed by Blockstream, designed to make it easier to integrate Bitcoin functions into applications. It provides low-level primitives for key management, transaction construction, address encoding and PSBT operations.

Libwally-core is written in C to be portable and performant, with *bindings* available for Python, Java, JavaScript and other languages. It relies on `libsecp256k1` for cryptographic operations on the elliptic curve.

It is notably used as a core dependency of Core Lightning (CLN) for all wallet- and transaction-related operations. Other projects such as Blockstream's Green Wallet also use it.

entries.title: LIGHTNING LABS
entries.body: A company founded in 2016 by Elizabeth Stark and Olaoluwa Osuntokun, specializing in developing infrastructure for the Lightning Network. Lightning Labs is the main maintainer of LND, one of the most widespread implementations of the Lightning protocol. The company also develops an ecosystem of complementary tools: Lightning Loop for *submarine swaps*, Lightning Pool for liquidity, Faraday for node analysis, Lightning Terminal for the graphical interface, and the Taproot Assets protocol for issuing assets on Bitcoin.

entries.title: LIGHTNING NETWORK
entries.body: A higher-layer protocol, built on top of the Bitcoin protocol, aimed at enabling fast, low-cost transactions. It allows the creation of payment channels between participants, within which transactions can be made almost instantly and with minimal fees, without having to record each individual transaction on the blockchain. Channels can remain open almost indefinitely, and only require on-chain transactions when they are opened and closed. The Lightning Network aims to improve Bitcoin's scalability and to make it possible to use it for low-value payments.

entries.title: LIGHTNING NETWORK+
entries.body:
Lightning Network+ is an online service that facilitates the creation of *liquidity swaps* on the Lightning Network. Several node operators coordinate to simultaneously open payment channels among themselves in a circular fashion, which guarantees that each of them receives as much inbound capacity as they offer. For example, 3 users A, B and C agree on the LN+ site on a *liquidity swap* of 1M sats: A opens a 1M sats channel to B, B does the same to C, and C in turn opens a channel to A.

This system thus makes it possible to improve the connectivity of one's Lightning node, while obtaining as much inbound liquidity as the outbound liquidity committed.

entries.title: LIGHTNING SERVICE PROVIDER
entries.body:
A company operating on Lightning whose business is to provide liquidity services to users. 

On Lightning, payments are made off-chain via bidirectional channels, whose capacity is limited by the funds locked in the on-chain 2/2 *multisig*. The main role of an LSP is to facilitate the management of this liquidity, either by helping to convert on-chain funds to Lightning, or by opening new channels to increase users' inbound capacity.

These services are often used by *non-custodial* wallets, so that the user can immediately receive Lightning payments without having to handle opening and managing channels themselves. In exchange, the LSP charges fees.

entries.title: LIGHTNING TERMINAL
entries.body:
A web graphical interface developed by Lightning Labs to administer a Lightning node. Lightning Terminal offers a visual dashboard for viewing the state of channels, liquidity, routed payments and node performance. It integrates the Loop, Pool and Faraday tools into a unified interface.

Lightning Terminal runs via the *litd* daemon and can be accessed remotely through the *Lightning Node Connect* (LNC) protocol, without requiring a VPN or complex network configuration. It is designed to simplify the day-to-day management of an LND node, by making accessible operations that usually require the command line.

entries.title: LIGHTSPARK
entries.body: A company co-founded by David Marcus, formerly head of PayPal and of the Libra/Diem project at Meta, with the mission of building an open payments infrastructure on Bitcoin. Lightspark first developed services and tools to facilitate integration of the Lightning Network, notably the UMA (*Universal Money Address*) protocol enabling interoperable transactions between institutions. The company then created Spark, a higher-layer protocol based on statechains, designed to overcome Lightning's limits regarding the scalability of self-custody wallets and stablecoin support. Lightspark also offers a *Wallet-as-a-Service* and stablecoin issuance platform leveraging Spark's capabilities.

entries.title: LIQUID NETWORK
entries.body: Bitcoin sidechain designed by Blockstream to provide fast and confidential transactions. Unlike the main Bitcoin blockchain, Liquid uses a consensus mechanism based on a federation (a selected group of node operators, generally Bitcoin-related companies), thereby replacing the Nakamoto consensus mechanism. This approach considerably speeds up transactions and reduces costs, while offering more advanced features. Liquid also allows the issuance of digital assets, including tokens representing other cryptocurrencies. The bitcoins on Liquid, called L-BTC, are tied to BTC through a two-way peg system relying on part of the federation. The participants in this federation are called “functionaries”, and they can take on both the role of “watchman” (*watchmen*) and of “block signer” (*blocksigner*).

entries.title: LIQUIDITY - LIGHTNING
entries.body: Refers to the capacity of a Lightning payment channel to pass transactions between two nodes depending on the bitcoins available on each side of the channel. There are two types of liquidity: inbound and outbound. Outbound liquidity represents the funds that the node can send or forward through the channel. Inbound liquidity represents the funds that it can receive or forward in the opposite direction. Liquidity can also refer to the sum of the liquidity available in all of a node's channels.

entries.title: LIQUIDITY ADS
entries.body: Mechanism of the Lightning Network protocol that allows node operators to advertise their willingness to provide inbound liquidity in exchange for compensation. A node that has funds can publish an offer on the network, specifying the amount of liquidity it is willing to allocate, the duration of the commitment, and the fee requested. When another node needs inbound capacity to receive payments, it can accept this offer and open a channel funded by the liquidity provider. This system creates an open and decentralized market for liquidity on Lightning, which solves a recurring problem for new nodes that cannot receive payments without inbound capacity. *Liquidity ads* have been formalized in the Lightning protocol specification, notably through the message `node_announcement` which allows nodes to advertise their offers, and the *dual funding* protocol (`open_channel2`) which allows the channel opening to be negotiated. This system makes it possible to automate the negotiation between the parties without a trusted intermediary.

entries.title: LIQUIDITY SWAP
entries.body:
Mechanism for coordinated opening of Lightning channels in which several node operators mutually commit to opening channels toward one another in a circular arrangement. Each participant opens a channel toward the next one in the circle, which guarantees that everyone obtains both inbound and outbound liquidity. This concept is also known as a “*ring of fire*”.

The LN+ platform is the most widely used service for organizing these exchanges. On this platform, the participants, generally between three and five, agree on an identical channel capacity. Once all the channels are open, the circle forms a loop in which each node has improved connectivity to the network. A circular rebalancing can then be performed to distribute the liquidity evenly across the channels.

entries.title: LITD
entries.body: Daemon (*daemon*) that bundles several Lightning Labs tools into a single process: LND, Loop, Pool, Faraday and Taproot Assets. By running *litd*, a node operator gains access to all of these services without having to install and configure them separately. The daemon also provides the Lightning Terminal web interface for administering the node, and exposes the *Lightning Node Connect* (LNC) protocol, allowing secure remote access from a web browser, without requiring complex network configuration such as a VPN or port forwarding.

entries.title: LITECOIN
entries.body: Altcoin created in 2011 by Charlie Lee, a former Google engineer. Litecoin (LTC) is a fork of the Bitcoin source code with a few parameter modifications: a block time reduced to 2.5 minutes instead of 10, a total number of units capped at 84 million (versus 21 million for Bitcoin), and the use of the Scrypt hashing algorithm instead of SHA-256 for proof of work. It has sometimes served as a testing ground for features later adopted by Bitcoin, such as SegWit, which was activated on Litecoin in May 2017, before being activated on Bitcoin in August of the same year.

entries.title: LITTLE-ENDIAN
entries.body: Data storage format in computer systems where the least significant bytes (the “little ends”) are placed first in address order. In a sequence of several bytes, the byte with the lowest weight (for example, the rightmost digits in hexadecimal) is stored first.

entries.title: LNBITS
entries.body:
Open source application that sits on top of any Lightning funding source (LND, Core Lightning, LNbits itself, etc.) and makes it possible to create isolated virtual wallets, each with its own API key. The main benefit is never exposing the total balance of the underlying node: each wallet only sees and can only spend the funds allocated to it, which makes it possible to delegate access to third-party applications without risk.

LNbits adopts a modular architecture where the core remains minimal and where all additional features are provided by optional extensions developed by the community: point of sale, payment links, *paywalls*, NIP-05 Nostr, *Bolt Cards*, payment terminals, *crowdfunding*, etc. Developers can create and share their own extensions. LNbits natively supports LNURL and Nostr, provides a complete REST API, and is accessible from a web browser.

entries.title: LNC - LIGHTNING NODE CONNECT
entries.body: Protocol developed by Lightning Labs that allows connecting remotely to a Lightning node via a proxy server, without exposing the node directly on the internet. LNC establishes an end-to-end encrypted connection between the client (for example Lightning Terminal in a browser) and the node, authenticating using a *pairing phrase*. This protocol eliminates the need to configure a VPN, open ports or manage TLS certificates, which considerably simplifies remote access to a personal node hosted behind a NAT or a firewall.

entries.title: LNCLI
entries.body: Command-line interface provided with LND to administer a Lightning node. LNCLI (*Lightning Network Command Line Interface*) allows executing RPC calls to the LND daemon to manage channels, send and receive payments, check balances, adjust routing fees and perform all the common operations of a node. Each command corresponds to an underlying gRPC call.

entries.title: LND
entries.body: Acronym for “*Lightning Network Daemon*”. It is a major implementation of the Lightning Network protocol written in the Go language. Developed by Lightning Labs, LND allows the creation and management of payment channels and nodes on the Lightning network.

entries.title: LNP/BP
entries.body: Swiss non-profit association founded in 2019 by Maxim Orlovsky and Giacomo Zucco. The acronym LNP/BP stands for “*Lightning Network Protocol / Bitcoin Protocol*”. The association is responsible for the development and maintenance of the standards of the RGB protocol, a smart contract system that operates with *client-side validation* on Bitcoin and the Lightning Network. RGB allows the issuance and transfer of digital assets and smart contracts directly on Bitcoin, keeping the data off-chain to preserve privacy and scalability. The association publishes and maintains a set of technical standards (LNPBP) that govern the operation of the protocol.

entries.title: LNP2PBOT
entries.body: Open source Telegram bot that allows buying and selling bitcoins peer-to-peer (P2P) via the Lightning Network. LNP2PBot works directly within the Telegram messaging application, where users can create buy or sell offers, and exchange bitcoins for local currencies. Transactions are carried out via the Lightning Network. An *escrow* system built into the bot secures the transactions: it temporarily holds the seller's sats until the buyer confirms the fiat payment.

entries.title: LNURL
entries.body:
Communication protocol that specifies a set of features designed to simplify interactions between Lightning nodes and clients, as well as third-party applications. This protocol is based on HTTP and allows creating links for various operations, such as a payment request, a withdrawal request, or other features that improve the user experience. Each LNURL is a URL encoded in bech32 with the prefix `lnurl`, which, once scanned, triggers a series of automatic actions on the Lightning wallet.

For example, the LNURL-withdraw feature (LUD-03) allows withdrawing funds from a service by scanning a QR code, without needing to manually generate an *invoice*. Or again, LNURL-auth (LUD-04) allows logging in to online services by using a private key on one's Lightning wallet instead of a password.

entries.title: LOCALBITCOINS
entries.body:
Peer-to-peer bitcoin exchange platform, founded in June 2012 by Jeremias Kangas in Finland. The service connected bitcoin buyers and sellers around the world, facilitating P2P transactions. Users posted ads specifying the amounts, prices and accepted payment methods (bank transfers, cash, online payment services...). An escrow system (*escrow*) protected both parties during the transaction. This model made it possible to exchange bitcoins for local currency in practically every country, including those lacking conventional exchange platforms.

LocalBitcoins shut down in February 2023, due to unfavorable market conditions and increasing regulation.

entries.title: LOCK
entries.body: File used in Bitcoin Core for locking the data directory. It is created when bitcoind or Bitcoin-qt starts to prevent several instances of the software from accessing the same data directory simultaneously. The purpose is to prevent conflicts and data corruption. The locking relies on an operating system lock mechanism applied to the file `.lock`. The file itself remains permanently present on the disk, but the lock is automatically released by the operating system when the process terminates, including in the event of an unexpected shutdown.

entries.title: LOOP
entries.body: Service developed by Lightning Labs designed to facilitate liquidity balancing in Lightning channels. Loop allows users to move funds between Bitcoin and the Lightning Network, without having to close or open a channel. Loop thus helps optimize one's liquidity and reduce the costs of managing one's channels.

entries.title: LOOP IN
entries.body: Operation offered by the Lightning Loop service that allows converting on-chain bitcoins into outbound liquidity in a Lightning channel. The user sends bitcoins on the blockchain and receives the equivalent (minus fees) in one of their Lightning channels via a *submarine swap*. *Loop In* is useful for increasing one's sending capacity on the Lightning Network, for example when a user has exhausted their outbound liquidity after making many payments and wants to be able to send more.

entries.title: LOOP OUT
entries.body: Operation offered by the Lightning Loop service that allows converting Lightning liquidity into on-chain bitcoins. The user makes a Lightning payment and receives the equivalent (minus fees) in their on-chain Bitcoin wallet via a *submarine swap*. *Loop Out* is useful for recovering funds on-chain without closing a channel, or for rebalancing liquidity by moving funds from a channel saturated on the outbound side to the on-chain wallet.

entries.title: LOTTERY MINING
entries.body:
Form of *solo mining* in which a miner uses a low-hashrate device to attempt to find a block on their own, without joining a pool. The probability of success is extremely low, but the reward, if a block is found, is collected in full by the miner.

The devices used are generally compact or open-source ASICs such as the Bitaxe, whose hashrate is around 0.5 to 1.2 TH/s depending on the model. At this power, the chances of solving a block are roughly one in several million per ten-minute period. Some miners connect to *solo mining* services such as Solo CKPool or Braiins Solo, which provide them with block *templates* and relay valid blocks to the network, without pooling the rewards.

The approach is more of a hobby than a profitable activity. Its adherents justify it by the contribution to the decentralization of the hashrate and by the appeal of a full reward in case of success.

entries.title: LUCK
entries.body:
Metric used in mining pools to measure a pool's performance relative to its theoretical expectations. As its name indicates, it evaluates how lucky the pool is at finding a block. Luck is calculated by comparing the number of shares theoretically required to find a valid block, based on Bitcoin's current difficulty, with the actual number of shares produced to find that block. A number of shares lower than expected indicates good luck, whereas a higher number indicates bad luck.

By relating Bitcoin's difficulty to the number of shares it produces each second and the difficulty of each share, the pool can calculate the number of shares that are theoretically required to find a valid block. For example, suppose that theoretically, 100,000 shares are needed for a pool to find a block. If the pool actually produces 200,000 before finding a block, its luck is 50%:

```text
100 000 / 200 000 = 0.5 = 50 %
```

Conversely, if this pool found a valid block after producing only 50,000 shares, then its luck is 200%:

```text
100 000 / 50 000 = 2 = 200 %
```

Luck is a metric that can only be updated after the pool discovers a block, which makes it a static metric that is updated periodically.

entries.title: LUD
entries.body: Acronym for "*LNURL Document*". LUDs are documents that define standardized protocols used within LNURL. Each LUD specifies a feature, such as payments (LUD-06), withdrawals (LUD-03) or authentication (LUD-04). They therefore allow good interoperability between the different Lightning services and clients using LNURL.

entries.title: LUXOR
entries.body: American company founded in 2017 by Nick Hansen, specializing in infrastructure services for Bitcoin mining. Luxor operates a pool, a custom firmware for ASICs (LuxOS), an analytics data platform (Hashrate Index), a hashrate derivatives desk and a marketplace for ASIC machines. The company primarily targets professional and institutional North American miners.

entries.title: THIERS' LAW
entries.body:
Economic principle that is the inverse of Gresham's law, according to which “good money drives out bad”. Formalized in 1989 by the economist Peter Bernholz in reference to the writings of the French historian Adolphe Thiers on the hyperinflation of the revolutionary assignats, this law describes a spontaneous market mechanism. When a currency deteriorates to the point of losing the confidence of economic agents, they end up refusing it in favor of a currency perceived as more reliable, despite legal constraints.

Thiers' law is mainly observed in situations of hyperinflation. When a national currency collapses, the laws imposing its legal tender status become ineffective: merchants demand to be paid in foreign currencies or in tangible goods. Historical examples include Zimbabwe, where the US dollar replaced the Zimbabwean dollar during its dollarization in 2009, or Weimar Germany, where the mark collapsed in 1923 to the point that trade was conducted in foreign currencies or by barter.

Some bitcoiners invoke Thiers' law to argue that Bitcoin could gradually establish itself as a medium of exchange in economies where the national currency is heavily depreciated, thus going beyond its sole role as a store of value.
